_comment: Forced-choice legibility set (CRITIC.md Mode 4). THIRTEEN PAIRS: each of seven positions gives exactly one idle and one action frame from the identical gameplay camera, so position carries zero information about which class a frame belongs to. A first attempt used one position for all twelve and produced six near-identical idle frames, which a critic can spot and use to infer the control without looking at the character. Every shot uses capture_when (advance until the player really is in that state) rather than capture_at (hand-tuned frame arithmetic, which silently broke when an 8-frame settle was added upstream), and every shot also declares expect_* so capture.gd fails the run on any mismatch. An earlier version of this set silently captured four 'idle' frames of a walking character. pair7 was added to cover a RENDERING FAULT rather than an animation: see its note. pairs 8-10 cover the axe, the bow draw and the shield; they are the only shots that change what the character is holding, and they do it with the F4 cycle_item action because a shot list has no other route into the game. Every shot sets lock_camera: the camera pivot is top_level and chases the player with a lerp, so an action that moves the character leaves the camera somewhere an idle frame does not. A blind critic caught exactly that ('the camera is not the same, it sits lower and closer'). capture.gd also freezes world Area3Ds for these runs, because teleporting the player between shots COLLECTED rupees and a matched pair ended up with different pickups in frame - also caught by a critic. Both were silent, and both broke the premise that the action is the only variable. Pairs 11-13 cover Z-target lock-on and the over-the-shoulder aim camera, and they are the first shots in this set whose control cannot use the same camera as its action: locking on and drawing a bow both move the camera on purpose, which is most of what they are for. Those shots carry `camera_from_game`, which tells tools/capture.gd to kill the follow lag as usual but to stop pinning yaw and pitch - without it a locked or aiming frame is silently reframed back to the walking camera and then shows neither state. Their controls state the locked camera's own measured angles by hand instead, so the framing matches and the lock is the variable. capture.gd also releases any held lock at the start of every shot, because Z-targeting is a toggle and would otherwise leak into the next control frame.

This was the weakest frame in the set and the only low-confidence call a critic made: charging runs inside the Idle state, so the pose WAS the idle pose and the only differences were the blade's colour and a soft ground glow — 'if the glow had been absent I would have called it IDLE with confidence 5 and been wrong'. There are now two hard-edged cues: a held anticipation pose (the `charge` clip, which is why expect_clip is no longer `idle`) and an outlined teal ground ring that closes inward. capture_offset waits 8 frames so the ring has finished converging — the charge is a HELD state, so any frame of it is representative, and the first frame of a 110 ms convergence is the least so.

shots._note: REGRESSION COVER for a rendering fault, not just another action frame. A spin on the river bank, where the expanding ground ring grows out over the water. A critic reported 'three or four thin black concentric arcs on the water surface with nothing inside them ... nobody would think spin attack; they would think the water is broken', and it was this: the ring is OPAQUE so it writes depth, the water is blend_mix so it erases the ring's fill without writing depth, and the outline pass — which reads the pre-transparent depth buffer — contoured a shape that was no longer visible. Diagnosed by freezing the frame and hiding one node at a time; with the ring hidden every arc vanished. actors/player/water_line.gd holds the fix and the full write-up. This pair exists so the fault cannot come back unnoticed: pair6 happens to be waterside too, but one position is a coincidence, two is coverage. The bank here sits BELOW the river surface, which is exactly the case a constant height offset cannot handle.
shots.name: pair7_action

shots._note: CONTROL for the AXE pair, and the first shot holding anything other than the sword. The loadout is advanced by the F4 `cycle_item` action, which is the only way a shot list can change what the character is holding: tools/capture.gd reaches the game through InputMap and nothing else. The cycle is SEQUENTIAL and persists across shots, so the order of the shots below is load-bearing — one press per pair, in the idle frame, which is also why the action frame of each pair needs none. Loadout.cycle() records the item as found WITHOUT the found banner, or a 30-point line of text would sit across the bottom of every frame here.
shots.name: pair8_idle

shots._note: The axe mid-swing, on the SAME clip the sword uses (slash_a) at 0.625x playback. Nothing about this frame is axe-specific code: the wind-up is 183 ms instead of 133 and the live window 167 instead of 100 because items/axe.tres asks for a slower rate. What a critic should be able to see is a top-heavy wedge rather than a straight blade, and a longer, deeper ribbon.
shots.name: pair8_action

shots._note: CONTROL for the BOW pair.
shots.name: pair9_idle

shots._note: THE HIGHEST-RISK FRAME IN THE SET, and it now has the camera the previous builder said it needed. A drawn bow is a HELD POSE WITH NO MOTION, structurally identical to the charge frame a critic called the weakest here: 'only the blade's colour changed - if the glow had been absent I would have called it IDLE with confidence 5 and been wrong'. Three cues were added on the character and none of them is a tint: both arms leaving the silhouette in OPPOSITE directions with the chest turned side-on, an opaque black-outlined arrow nocked on the string, and - at full draw only - the same hard-edged ground ring the sword's charge uses. But the structural limit was the camera, and that was measured rather than argued: from directly behind the character the DRAW AXIS IS THE VIEW AXIS, so the nocked arrow's 0.42 m retraction covered 18 px of screen and the bow's silhouette stayed a 3-5 px line whichever way you looked at it. PlayerAimState now brings the camera over the right shoulder - 2.7 m out, 0.95 m across, FOV 64 - which measures 66 px of nock travel and a 2.29x larger bow. `camera_from_game` is what lets that survive to the frame: without it tools/capture.gd pins the pivot back above the player and the pitch back to -20 while the spring is still at 2.4 m, producing a close-up with no shoulder offset that is neither camera. capture_offset 44 puts this past the 500 ms draw and past the ring's 110 ms convergence, so it is a FULL draw; pair13 is the partial one.
shots.name: pair9_action

shots._note: CONTROL for the SHIELD pair.
shots.name: pair10_idle

shots._note: Shield up. Also a held pose with no motion, and the same risk as the bow draw. The slab is raised ABOVE AND OUTSIDE THE RIGHT SHOULDER rather than held in front of the chest, which is deliberate: CLAUDE.md records that the only screen space an over-the-shoulder camera does not already own is above the head and outside the shoulders, and a 0.68 x 0.88 m board held in front of a 1.34 m torso is a board the camera looks THROUGH the character to see. With one equip slot this frame also has to answer 'what am I holding', because nothing else does.
shots.name: pair10_action

shots._note: CONTROL for the LOCKED pair, and the first shot back on the sword: one cycle_item press takes the loadout from the shield pair10 left it holding round to the sword. camera_yaw_deg -175.9 and camera_pitch_deg -35.8 are the angles the locked camera actually settles to from this spot, so the control frames the same two dummies from the same place and the lock is the only thing missing. A CAVEAT ON THIS PAIR, stated rather than hidden: pairs 1-10 are strict forced-choice pairs whose only variable is what the character is doing, and this one cannot be. Z-targeting IS a camera change - it yaws round behind the player onto the target and solves the pitch that lands the target at a quarter of the frame height - so the control states the same yaw and pitch by hand, measured off a headless run rather than guessed, and the honest remaining differences are the reticle, the 0.45 m pivot lift, and the character facing the target instead of the camera. Judge it as 'is it obvious what I am locked onto', not as a coin flip. WHY THESE SHOTS FACE NORTH, into the forest gate, rather than south over the open field: they were tried the other way and the lock refused to acquire, for a reason worth writing down. The clearing is wrapped in an invisible `Bounds` StaticBody on the WORLD layer at z = ±24.5. Standing north of the dummies puts the camera eye at z 24.6-25.9, i.e. OUTSIDE that wall, so every sight-line from the camera back into the level is blocked by it and LockOnSystem correctly reports the target as hidden. In real play this never happens, because the SpringArm also masks the world layer and simply shortens against the wall — but `lock_camera` disables arm collision to keep paired frames the same distance apart, which is exactly what pushes the eye through it. The dummies sit at z 13-15.5 so they stay behind every one of the twenty older shots' cameras, and that leaves no room to stand north of them and still be 5 m back. So the background here is the gate and the lookout cliffs, which is busier than the field and is a known weakness of these two frames rather than a hidden one. A LAST DETAIL that took a look at the frame to notice: the control walks north for sixteen frames before it is photographed. Without that it stood facing the LENS, because an idle unlocked character keeps whatever yaw it last moved with and a teleported one has none — so the pair differed by the character's whole facing for a reason that had nothing to do with locking on. Walking first means both frames face the same way and the honest differences are only the reticle and the pivot lift. It also forces `capture_at` rather than `capture_when`, for the reason pair13_idle records: `capture_when` breaks the input timeline the instant it matches, and 'is the player idle' is true on frame one.
shots.name: pair11_idle

shots._note: LOCKED ON, standing still - the frame that answers 'is it obvious what I am locked onto'. Two straw dummies stand 3.4 m apart in the sparring ground; the one that gets locked is 7.11 m away and the one that does not is 4.88 m away, because selection is screen-space distance from the centre of frame and never 3D range. So this frame is also the visible proof of that rule: if the reticle is on the NEAR dummy, the load-bearing decision in components/lockon_system.gd has been quietly rewritten. capture_offset 40 puts it past the 367 ms camera settle and past the reticle's 110 ms convergence, so the brackets have finished closing - a reticle caught mid-converge is the least representative frame of a held state.
shots.name: pair11_action

shots._note: A SWING WITH A TARGET, and the reason three separate findings all ended at lock-on. A critic missed an attack outright because a signpost ate the arc, and noted that 'props like signs and chests are exactly what you swing next to'; a builder then proved no VFX can fix it, because clearing the body at chest height needs the camera 3.3 m to the side and occlusion is a property of the sight-line rather than of the frustum. God of War 2018's systemic answer is what is in this frame: with a target the character is rotated onto it on the frame the swing is committed - measured at 0.000 degrees of error against 45.000 unlocked - and the camera is already looking down the same line. So the arc is presented the same way every time instead of wherever the stick happened to point, and it sweeps into the volume the framing deliberately leaves open between player and target. Measured: a signpost-sized prop placed on the sight-line covers 9 of 9 blade samples unlocked and 0 of 9 locked. Target pressed at frame 1 and the swing 30 frames later, so the camera has settled before the blade moves - REFERENCE.md's cross-check is that camera settle, 367 ms, must come in under attack commitment, 417 ms.
shots.name: pair12_action

shots._note: CONTROL for the PARTIAL bow draw. Two cycle_item presses take the loadout from the sword round through the axe to the bow, and this is the only shot in the set that uses `capture_at` rather than `capture_when` -- deliberately, because `capture_when` breaks the input timeline the moment it matches, and 'is the player idle' is true on frame 1. The first version of this shot therefore fired one of its two cycle presses, arrived holding the AXE, and the run failed on pair13_action reaching the `charge` clip instead of `bow_draw`. With no capture_when the timeline runs to frame 20 and both presses land; expect_state and expect_clip still guard the frame, which is what capture_when was really for. Shot from the ordinary walking camera, because that is what the aim camera is being compared against -- the camera IS part of the aim state, the same caveat pairs 11 and 12 carry.
shots.name: pair13_idle

shots._note: A PARTIAL draw, over the shoulder - the frame pair9's builder named as the one to add next, because a half-drawn bow is a weaker read by design and is exactly where the cue that carries the draw's PROGRESS has to do its work. capture_offset 12 lands roughly half way through the 500 ms draw, by which point the shoulder rig is about 94% blended in. The question here is narrower than pair9's: not 'is this person holding a bow' but 'is the string back, and how far'. There is also a dummy 11 m ahead, so this frame has something to be aimed AT, which pair9's does not. The position moved once for a reason only the frame showed: at the first spot a rupee sat squarely over the character's chest, i.e. over the bow's grip, which is the one region of that frame that had to read.
shots.name: pair13_action
